description: We are Álvaro, Ricardo, Joel, María, Mariano and Gonzalo. We look forward to have a lot of fun at the Space Apps Challenge.
summary:
When we saw the challenge of how to help astronauts survive on Mars, we thought, How can we create a training tool to simulate critical situations before they leave Earth?

And we came up with S.A.R.A. (Super Artificial Robotic Intelligence, named after Spanish astronaut Sara García Alonso), a rehearsal tool for astronauts exploring Jezero Crater on Mars.

It combines NASA data from multiple missions: HiRISE topography and imagery (MRO) and Perseverance weather measurements (MEDA), into a 3D terrain view where crews can plan an EVA route that accounts for slope, distance from shelter, and consumables.

An onboard AI assistant, guided by a draft set of Mars surface flight rules adapted from NASA Shuttle and ISS flight rules, advises the crew in critical scenarios such as dust storms, power loss, or communication blackouts, accounting for Earth–Mars signal delay, acting as a coach who explains what to do.

Its goal is astronaut safety: crews rehearse the hardest situations before leaving and use the same tool on the surface.
details:
What does it do?

It recreates in VR what an astronaut would experience on Mars, performing several missions to explore the western delta of Jezero Crater, where Perseverance has been collecting samples. We chose Jezero because it was once an ancient lake, and its sediments may preserve signs of past life. Our science objective is to collect a sediment core from the delta.

It includes an AI assistant called SARA, named after the Spanish astronaut Sara García. This voice assistant follows a summary we made of real NASA flight rules to make it as accurate as possible. It guides you along the mission, solves doubts, and gives instructions in critical moments.

The missions put this to the test. In ARES-01 The Last Sample, a dust storm hits mid-drill, and the astronaut must secure the equipment and walk 350 m back to the rover, taking a 65 m detour around unstable ground. In ARES-02 Nightfall Protocol, the astronaut drives at night to a remote station.

Our main objective is to help astronauts prepare for difficult missions on Mars by rehearsing as much as possible beforehand and to support them during the mission itself through the helmet display and SARA.

How would it help a real astronaut?

It would help rehearse the protocols for critical situations or accidents and help with mental preparation.

During the mission, the AI assistant always knows the live distance and direction back to the rover, and it recommends ending the EVA early when the return becomes unsafe. A signal from Mars takes between 4 and 22 minutes to reach Earth, so SARA gives immediate answers when Mission Control can't, while the astronaut keeps the final call.

The AI assistant can also activate an infrared mode to see during dust storms and turn on a danger layer showing unsafe ground (unstable soil, steep slopes and poor visibility). It can zoom the map in and out and turn the helmet flashlight on and off. This helps the astronaut by allowing them to focus entirely on the mission, hands-free.

The main factors we considered were astronaut safety, accuracy (reflected in the data and sources), and simulating the Mars experience for astronauts and the wider public while keeping the experience immersive.

What resources did we use?

- TypeScript: the language for all the app code. Its type checking caught errors across the visor, SARA, and the server.

- SvelteKit + Svelte 5: the web framework. It provides the pages (the visor, the missions and the operator panel), the UI components, and the server routes for SARA.

- three.js + WebXR: three.js renders the 3D Jezero terrain, the rocks, the sky, the dust, and the models in the browser. WebXR runs the same scene in VR on the Meta Quest 2.

- Vite: the build tool and development server.

- Cloudflare Workers: hosting. It serves the site and runs SARA's server routes, which keeps the API keys secret, all on HTTPS (required for the headset microphone).

- Claude Haiku 5.5 (Anthropic): SARA's brain. It answers using the telemetry, mission state, MEDA weather, and flight rules, and calls tools to control the map, the infrared and danger layers, and the flashlight.

- Groq Whisper: speech-to-text. It turns the astronaut's push-to-talk audio into text.

- ElevenLabs: text-to-speech. It gives SARA her voice and pre-recorded the fixed alert lines.

- Python and Node.js pipelines: scripts that turn raw NASA data into compact files for the browser.

- NASA 3D Resources: real NASA models placed in the scene. The Space Exploration Vehicle is the pressurised rover, the Mars 2020 sample tube is the survey samples, and the Habitat Demonstration Unit is Bravo Station.

The hardware we used was our own laptops to code and the Meta Quest 2 VR headset to test and deploy the simulator.

We used multi-agent workflows with Claude Code, Codex, and Opencode to help us create this program.

Why is it accurate?

We built as much as we could using real NASA data.

- Terrain is a HiRISE elevation model and orthomosaic of the Jezero delta, and the geology comes from the USGS geologic map SIM 3464 (Sun and Stack, 2020).

- Weather values are real Perseverance MEDA measurements from the NASA Planetary Data System, replayed at the scene's local solar time and season. The dust storm uses the real January 2022 record from sol 313.

- The danger layer we created combines geology, slope, surface roughness, ground temperature, and dust visibility.

- SARA follows condensed, real, documented NASA practice: the Apollo walkback limit and 30-minute reserve, ISS EVA 23 (2013), and NEEMO communication-delay studies.

- Almost all the 3D models we used come from NASA.

- Anything we could not measure, such as the suit telemetry, the infrared view and the mission storyline, is labelled as simulated.

We tried to take a different path by creating something that can be used both before and during the mission, using a VR headset, and implementing AI in a useful way.

The first humans on Mars won't have Mission Control in real time. We built the crewmate that can be there.

Considerations:

This is a project we created in two days and can still be polished in many details
